title: Farid: don't strike back
hook: if someone hits you, don't hit back; kiss their feet and go home (Farid salok, ang 1378)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Farid of Pakpattan, the Sufi whose verses the Gurus kept. Your line was the first punjabi voice. Did his jewel line guard your words? Today, one of his hardest sayings, and the end of a week. Day two hundred fifty-nine.
screen: `FARID OF PAKPATTAN — THE FIRST PUNJABI VOICE.`

segments.voice: Someone cuts you off in traffic, then leans on the horn as if it was your fault. Or a relative makes the comment, the one they always make, in front of everyone. You feel it rise in your chest: the perfect comeback, the return honk, the thing that'll put them in their place. It's so satisfying for about four seconds. Then you carry it home and chew on it all night. Sheikh Farid, eight hundred years ago, had a couplet for exactly this moment. Today, Farid: don't strike back.
screen: `THE HORN, THE COMMENT.` → `THE PERFECT COMEBACK RISES.` → `FOUR SECONDS, THEN ALL NIGHT.`

segments.voice: On Ang 1378, among Farid's saloks: fareedaa je tai maaran mukeeaan tinhaa na maare ghumm; aapnarai ghar jaaeeai pair tinhaa de chumm. Farid, if someone strikes you with their fists, don't strike them back. Kiss their feet, and go home. It's startling. Kiss their feet? In Farid's Punjab, touching or kissing the feet was a gesture of deep respect and humility. He's asking for the opposite of revenge: meet the blow with humility, then walk away to your own home, your own peace, without carrying the fight with you. Farid isn't saying the blow was fine, or that wrong doesn't matter. The saloks around this one are about humility and not letting anger into the mind. And many readers notice the last line: go home. Don't stand there and take more. Don't keep the quarrel alive. Leave it. Now, four days ago, Kabir praised the hero who fights for the helpless. So which is it? Many Sikhs hold the two together this way. When the blow is against you, your own pride, your own honor, you can let it go and go home. When the helpless are being crushed, you stand on the field. The ego doesn't get to fight for itself; the weak get defended. That's the whole week, in a way: a weaver whose loom was prayer, one light in everyone, a warrior for the helpless, a death that delights, Kabir's short sharp saloks, and Farid, the first Punjabi voice, telling us to go home in peace.
screen: `JE TAI MAARAN MUKEEAAN — IF STRUCK.` · `KISS THEIR FEET: HUMILITY, NOT REVENGE.` · `AAPNARAI GHAR — GO HOME.` · `FOR YOURSELF, LET GO; FOR OTHERS, STAND.` · then, large: `GO HOME IN PEACE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one slight you're still carrying: a comment, a snub, a small unfairness from this week. Notice where it sits in your body. Then picture yourself, like Farid says, bowing slightly to it, and turning, and walking home. The door closes behind you. The fight stays outside. Breathe out, and let your shoulders drop. The bell holds the time.

Farid. Here, his salok: if someone strikes you, don't strike back; meet it with humility and go home. This week: Kabir the weaver, one light, the true warrior, the death that delights, saloks, Farid of Pakpattan, and Farid again.
Your line: go home in peace. Today, let one slight go, and don't carry it home with you. Day two hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Farid's saloks are read in the Guru Granth Sahib and often quoted by Sikhs about humility and forgiveness in personal quarrels, alongside the Sikh duty to defend others who are wronged.

fork.setup: someone strikes you in a quarrel. what does Farid's salok say to do?
options: don't strike back; meet it with humility and go home.
stay and argue until they apologize.
fork.reveal: tinhaa na maare ghumm... aapnarai ghar jaaeeai: don't hit back, kiss their feet, and go home in peace.

original.note: Gurmukhi: fareedaa, O Farid, the way his saloks address himself.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't strike back means let people walk all over you.
what it means: meet a blow against your own pride with humility, then leave, and don't carry the fight home.

what a scholar hears: Salok Farid 7, Ang 1378; ghumm is a blow or punch, and pair chumm, kissing the feet, is a gesture of humility; read alongside Kabir's sooraa salok, Sikh commentators separate personal revenge from defending others.
